overview: Daspletosaurus torosus ("frightful lizard") was a large tyrannosaurine from the Late Campanian of Alberta (~76–77 Ma), contemporaneous with Gorgosaurus in the Dinosaur Park Formation. The co-occurrence of two large tyrannosaurs in the same formation is unusual and has generated competing hypotheses about ecological partitioning, temporal replacement and niche separation.

Daspletosaurus was more robust and had proportionally larger teeth than Gorgosaurus, suggesting it may have specialised on larger, more heavily armoured prey such as ceratopsids. A recently described species, D. wilsoni, from the Oldman Formation represents an older member of the lineage, suggesting a continuous tyrannosaurine presence in the region.

fossilSites.note: Campanian deposits co-preserving Daspletosaurus and Gorgosaurus — the classic "two large tyrannosaur" formation.

fossilSites.name: Oldman Formation
fossilSites.note: Older Campanian beds with Daspletosaurus wilsoni, documenting the earlier evolutionary history of the lineage.

articles.title: Discovery
articles.body: Russell described Daspletosaurus torosus in 1970 from a nearly complete skeleton collected by Charles Sternberg from the Dinosaur Park Formation. The species name "torosus" refers to its robust muscular build. Additional specimens have since been recovered, and D. wilsoni was described in 2022.

articles.title: Niche partitioning with Gorgosaurus
articles.body: The two large tyrannosaurs differ in robustness: Daspletosaurus has a deeper, heavier skull and more powerful dentition consistent with regularly attacking heavily built prey. Gorgosaurus is more gracile, possibly pursuing lighter-bodied hadrosaurs. Whether they partitioned prey by size or used habitats differently remains an active research question.

articles.title: Evolutionary significance
articles.body: Daspletosaurus is placed in Tyrannosaurinae alongside Tarbosaurus and Tyrannosaurus, suggesting a northern Laurasian origin of this clade. Its presence in Alberta predating both Tarbosaurus in Asia and Tyrannosaurus in North America places it near the ancestral node of the iconic Late Cretaceous large tyrannosaur radiation.

fossilRecord.evidence: A robust skull and strong teeth distinguish Daspletosaurus from the slimmer Gorgosaurus with which it coexisted.

record.mya: late Campanian, approximately 77-74 million years ago
record.description: Daspletosaurus was a large tyrannosaurine predator from Campanian rocks of western North America. D. torosus is known from multiple skulls and partial skeletons, while newer named species and proposed anagenetic succession remain actively debated.
facts: The genus has strong cranial and postcranial evidence from multiple individuals.
Bonebeds and close associations do not by themselves prove permanent pack hunting.
Species-level ranges and assignments should be stated separately rather than merged into one long genus average.

review.ageReviewNote: D. torosus is concentrated in the Oldman Formation near 77-76 Ma; younger Daspletosaurus material may represent other species.
